title: Crossing the Cervico-Thoracic Junction in Long Posterior Cervical Fusions Reduces Caudal Adjacent Segment Pathology
condition_or_topic: Clinically symptomatic caudal adjacent segment pathology (ASP) after long posterior cervical fusion (PCF).
clinical_background: Long PCF is used for multilevel radiculopathy or myelopathy, particularly in revision surgery. Although decompression and stabilization can yield favorable outcomes, the long construct may contribute to ASP over time. Extending the fusion across the cervico-thoracic junction might reduce caudal ASP because the rib cage stabilizes adjacent thoracic levels, but the authors state that evidence supporting this practice was lacking.
objectives: Compare clinical outcomes and rates of clinically symptomatic caudal ASP between long PCF constructs ending in the cervical spine and those ending in the proximal thoracic spine.
clinical_question: In patients undergoing long PCF, does a construct ending in the proximal thoracic spine, compared with one ending in the cervical spine, reduce clinically symptomatic caudal ASP and improve clinical outcomes?
study_design: Retrospective case-control study based on a review of consecutive cervical fusion cases performed by a single surgeon at one institution. Following Institutional Review Board approval, 2 surgeons who had not participated in patient care analyzed the data.

population.description: The review covered 1,714 consecutive cervical spinal fusion cases. The compared groups comprised 36 patients with a cervical end-instrumented vertebra (age 56 + 10 yrs) and 53 patients with a thoracic end-instrumented vertebra (age 57 + 9 yrs).
inclusion_criteria: Consecutive patients undergoing a minimum 3-level PCF that included at least the C5 vertebra.
population.care_setting: Single institution; procedures performed by a single surgeon.

interventions: Minimum 3-level PCF crossing the cervico-thoracic junction, with the distal instrumented level at T1 (n = 22), T2 (n = 12), T3 (n = 11), or T4 (n = 8); EIV-T group.
comparators: Minimum 3-level PCF ending in the cervical spine, with the distal instrumented level at C5 (n = 4), C6 (n = 10), or C7 (n = 22); EIV-C group.

primary: Frequency of clinically symptomatic caudal ASP, defined by revision surgery involving the caudal adjacent level or interventional pain treatment for pathology at that level, including recommended surgery or injection.
Clinical outcomes, including Neck Disability Index (NDI) score at 2 years follow up.
secondary: Radiographic measures associated with clinically symptomatic caudal ASP.

follow_up: Inclusion required at least 2 years follow-up; the reported average was 35 Months (range 18-82 Months). NDI was assessed at 2 years follow up.
interpretation: In this cohort, long PCF constructs extending across the C-T junction were associated with significantly less clinically symptomatic caudal ASP requiring intervention and better clinical outcomes than constructs ending in the cervical spine. Thoracic-ending constructs involved more fused levels and greater EBL, without significant differences in operative time or complication rates. The authors interpret the lower caudal ASP rate despite the longer constructs as evidence of a protective effect from crossing the junction.
comparison_with_prior_evidence: Earlier studies identified leaving C5-6 and C6-7 unfused as a risk factor for ASP after cervical fusion; the authors consider their findings consistent with those reports, while noting that their cohort underwent a posterior-only approach. A separate study at their institution linked sagittal malalignment after anterior cervical fusion to more symptomatic ASP, but the authors did not establish whether that finding applies to PCF. As background, they cite Hilibrand et al. for a 2.9% annual incidence of symptomatic ASP and 25.6% newly symptomatic ASP within 10 years after anterior cervical fusion. They also cite biomechanical work by Prasarn et al. and Hussain et al. concerning adjacent-segment effects of multilevel fusion, and a study by Lee et al. of 1358 cervical spine surgery cases reporting that posterior fusion carried 3 times the risk of revision for ASP compared with anterior fusion.
clinical_implications: Crossing the C-T junction may protect caudal adjacent levels in long PCF, which the authors relate to stabilization by the rib cage.
The potential reduction in symptomatic caudal ASP must be weighed against the greater fusion length and EBL; avoiding ASP should not take precedence over all other surgical goals.
practice_implications: The authors now seriously consider extending long instrumented posterior cervical arthrodeses across the cervico-thoracic junction rather than stopping at C7.

They recommend deciding whether the distal instrumented vertebra should be cervical or thoracic on a case-by-case basis, considering the effect on ASP alongside other factors when selecting levels and counseling patients.
For young patients seeking to preserve motion when future surgery would not pose undue risk, the authors suggest that treating only symptomatic levels may be advisable.
For some frail or very elderly patients, the authors suggest that a shorter construct may be advisable because a longer one could pose greater risks.
limitations: Radiographic outcomes were not correlated with the study results apart from changes in lordosis.
The study was a retrospective review of a consecutive series from one surgeon and included varied surgical indications.
The timing of symptomatic caudal ASP development was not compared between groups.
The definition of clinically symptomatic caudal ASP excluded patients with less severe symptoms managed with medication and physical therapy alone.
Patients with radiographic ASP but no clinical symptoms were excluded.
Clinically symptomatic cranial ASP was not analyzed; cranial extension during revision could occur without cranial symptoms, complicating its identification.
The groups differed significantly in the number of fused levels.
strengths: The authors describe this as the first comparison of clinically symptomatic caudal ASP after long PCF according to whether the construct crosses the cervico-thoracic junction.
The series was consecutive and performed by a single surgeon, with data reviewed by 2 independent surgeons who had not participated in patient care.
open_questions: Whether sagittal alignment after PCF influences symptomatic ASP as reported in a separate study of anterior cervical fusion remains unresolved.
Whether the groups differ in when clinically symptomatic caudal ASP develops remains unknown.
future_directions: Conduct a radiographic study to examine whether the reported relationship between sagittal malalignment and symptomatic ASP also holds after PCF.
Consider a prospective randomized trial in a more narrowly defined clinical cohort.
Use prospective follow-up to compare the timing of symptomatic caudal ASP between groups and better understand its pathogenesis.

main_findings.description: Clinically symptomatic caudal ASP requiring intervention occurred more frequently when the fusion ended in the cervical spine than when it ended in the thoracic spine.
main_findings.context: Table 3 reports the corresponding rates as 38.9% and 14.8%, respectively. The table labels the EIV-thoracic group n = 53 but uses 54 as the denominator for this outcome.

main_findings.description: Caudal extension of the fusion did not differ significantly between groups.
main_findings.context: Table 3 labels the EIV-thoracic group n = 53 but uses 54 as the denominator for this outcome.

main_findings.description: Caudal ASP injections, whether performed or recommended, were more frequent in the cervical-ending group.
main_findings.context: Table 3 labels the EIV-thoracic group n = 53 but uses 54 as the denominator for this outcome.

main_findings.description: Neck Disability Index outcomes at the postoperative assessment favored the thoracic-ending group significantly.

safety_results.overall_adverse_events: Overall complication rates were reported as similar: EIV-C 8/36 (22.2%) Vs. EIV-T 10/53 (18.5%). Surgical revision rates were also described as similar, without separate rates.

subgroup_analyses: By distal fusion level, caudal-level ASP occurred at C7 (41%), C6 (40%), C5 (25%), T1 (18%), T3 (18%), T2 (17%), and T4 (0%), in the order reported.
The EIV-C group ended at C5 (n = 4), C6 (n = 10), or C7 (n = 22); the EIV-T group ended at T1 (n = 22), T2 (n = 12), T3 (n = 11), or T4 (n = 8).
secondary_results: Fusion length was greater in EIV-thoracic than EIV-cervical: total levels fused were 7.0 + 2.7 versus 3.9 + 0.9, respectively; P-value <0.001.
EBL (mL) was higher in EIV-thoracic than EIV-cervical: 343 + 242 versus 206 + 54, respectively; P-value <0.001.
Operative Time (min) did not differ significantly: EIV-cervical 180 + 65 and EIV-thoracic 196 + 70; P-value NS.

For patients with available, measurable complete x-rays, the preoperative C3-C7 Angle was EIV-cervical 1.8 + 9.0 and EIV-thoracic 2.0 + 11.3; P-value 0.35. The groups comprised n = 14 and n = 25, respectively.
For those radiographic groups, the postoperative C3-C7 Angle was EIV-cervical 4.3 + 9.5 and EIV-thoracic 0.6 + 10.8; P-value 0.08.

For those radiographic groups, the final follow-up C3-C7 Angle was EIV-cervical 4.7 + 8.7 and EIV-thoracic 0.5 + 10.9; P-value 0.05. The authors nevertheless describe changes in cervical lordosis as not statistically significant.
Baseline age was EIV-C 55.8 + 10.3 and EIV-T 56.6 + 9.0; P-value NS.
At baseline, the male proportions were EIV-C 20/36 (56%) and EIV-T 26/54 (49%); P-value NS. Table 1 labels the EIV-T group n = 53 but uses 54 as the denominator.
At baseline, myelopathy was reported for EIV-C 3/36 (8%) and EIV-T 6/54 (11%); P-value NS.
At baseline, radiculopathy was reported for EIV-C 19/36 (53%) and EIV-T 33/54 (62%); P-value NS.
Myeloradiculopathy was a more frequent baseline indication in EIV-C: 11/36 (31%) versus EIV-T 6/54 (11%); P-value 0.03.
Primary surgery was reported for EIV-C 10/36 (28%) and EIV-T 8/54 (15%); P-value NS.
All except 2 EIV-C patients and 8 EIV-T patients had undergone anterior cervical fusion previously or concurrently with posterior fusion.
In EIV-C, 5 patients underwent laminoplasty and 6 underwent laminectomy; in EIV-T, 2 patients underwent laminoplasty and 14 underwent laminectomy.

main_conclusion: The authors conclude that extending a long PCF across the C-T junction is associated with less clinically symptomatic caudal ASP and better clinical outcomes at 2 years, despite longer constructs and greater EBL. They report no significant increase in operative time or complications and emphasize that the choice of distal fusion level remains individualized.
narrative_summary:
This retrospective case-control study examined whether the distal extent of a long PCF was associated with clinically symptomatic caudal ASP. From 1,714 consecutive cervical fusion cases at one institution, the authors compared 36 patients whose instrumentation ended in the cervical spine with 53 whose constructs extended into the proximal thoracic spine. Eligible patients underwent at least a 3-level PCF and had at least 2 years of follow-up. Symptomatic caudal ASP was defined by revision surgery, injection, or a recommendation for surgery or injection at the adjacent level.

Caudal ASP requiring intervention was more frequent with a cervical endpoint than with a thoracic endpoint (39% vs 15%, p = 0.01). At 2 years, Neck Disability Index outcomes favored the thoracic group (24.5 vs. 34.0, p = 0.05). Thoracic constructs fused more levels and had greater EBL, while operative times and overall complication rates were similar. The authors interpret crossing the C-T junction as protective against symptomatic caudal breakdown, but caution that preserving motion or avoiding the risks of a longer construct may matter more for some patients. Interpretation is limited by the retrospective, single-surgeon design, differing fusion lengths, and exclusion of asymptomatic radiographic ASP and less severe symptoms managed without injection or revision. The tables also use an EIV-thoracic heading of n = 53 alongside several outcome denominators of 54.

document_sections.heading: Abstract
document_sections.content: This retrospective case-control study compared clinical outcomes and symptomatic caudal adjacent segment pathology (ASP) after posterior cervical fusions (PCF) ending in the cervical spine (EIV-C) or proximal thoracic spine (EIV-T). A review of 1714 consecutive cervical fusion cases identified 36 EIV-C patients (age 56 + 10 yrs) and 53 EIV-T patients (age 57 + 9 yrs). Symptomatic ASP meant revision surgery, a nerve-root injection, or a recommendation for surgery or injection at an adjacent level. Caudal ASP requiring intervention was more frequent with EIV-C than EIV-T (39% vs 15%, p = 0.01); its frequency was greatest at C7 (41%) and then C6 (40%). Overall complications and surgical revisions were similar. At 2 years postop, Neck Disability Index results favored EIV-T (24.5 vs. 34.0, p = 0.05). The authors conclude that crossing the C-T junction improves clinical outcomes and reduces caudal adjacent-level deterioration, while requiring longer fusions and greater EBL but without increasing complications, operative time or morbidity significantly.

document_sections.heading: Introduction
document_sections.content: Long PCF is commonly used for multilevel radiculopathy, myelopathy, or both, particularly during revision surgery. The operative aims are decompression and stabilization without fusing more segments than necessary. ASP can arise over time despite stable imaging and good outcomes after cervical decompression and stabilization; the long lever arm may contribute. The authors propose that the ribs stabilize levels below a construct crossing the cervico-thoracic junction and might therefore reduce symptomatic caudal ASP. They state that supporting data were unavailable. Their objective was to compare clinical outcomes and symptomatic caudal ASP between long PCF constructs ending in the cervical spine and those ending in the proximal thoracic spine. They hypothesized that crossing the junction would lower symptomatic ASP relative to ending in the distal cervical spine.

document_sections.heading: Methods
document_sections.content: This was a retrospective review of 1,714 consecutive cervical fusion cases performed by one surgeon at one institution. After Institutional Review Board (IRB) approval, 2 surgeons who had not cared for the patients independently assessed the data. Eligible patients had a PCF spanning at least 3 levels, follow-up of at least 2 years, and a construct that included at least C5. The comparison included 36 EIV-C patients (age 56 + 10 yrs) and 53 EIV-T patients (age 57 + 9 yrs), each treated with a minimum 3-level PCF. Average follow-up was 35 Months, with a range of 18-82 Months. Distal fusion levels in EIV-C were C5 (n = 4), C6 (n = 10) and C7 (n = 22); in EIV-T they were T1 (n = 22), T2 (n = 12), T3 (n = 11) and T4 (n = 8). Comparisons covered perioperative measures, the incidence and radiographic features of clinically symptomatic caudal ASP, and Neck Disability Index (NDI) at 2 years follow up. Clinically symptomatic caudal ASP meant revision surgery involving the caudal adjacent level or interventional pain management for pathology there, including recommended surgery or injection. Incidence was examined by end-instrumented vertebra.

document_sections.heading: Results
document_sections.content: At baseline, age, sex and the number of primary surgeries did not differ between groups, whereas myeloradiculopathy was a more frequent indication in EIV-C. EIV-T had significantly longer constructs and higher EBL, without a significant operative-time difference. Prior or concurrent anterior cervical fusion had been performed in all but 2 EIV-C patients and all but 8 EIV-T patients. In EIV-C, 5 patients underwent laminoplasty and 6 underwent laminectomy; in EIV-T, 2 patients underwent laminoplasty and 14 underwent laminectomy. Clinically symptomatic caudal ASP requiring intervention was significantly more frequent in EIV-C than EIV-T (39% vs 15%, p = 0.01). Complete, measurable radiographs were available for 14 EIV-C patients and 25 EIV-T patients; changes in cervical lordosis did not differ statistically between groups. At 2 years postop, Neck Disability Index outcomes were significantly better in EIV-T than EIV-C (24.5 vs 34.0, p = 0.05). Caudal-level ASP occurred most frequently when the construct ended at C7 (41%), followed by C6 (40%), C5 (25%), T1 (18%), T3 (18%), T2 (17%) and T4 (0%). Overall complication and surgical revision rates were described as similar: EIV-C 8/36 (22.2%) Vs. EIV-T 10/53 (18.5%).

document_sections.heading: Discussion
document_sections.content: Long PCF is commonly indicated for multilevel degenerative, traumatic, neoplastic and congenital cervical conditions. ASP remains possible despite favorable clinical and radiographic outcomes and may relate to the long lever arm. The authors suggest that thoracic rib-cage stabilization could protect the caudal adjacent level when a construct crosses the cervico-thoracic junction. In their comparison, symptomatic caudal ASP requiring intervention was significantly more frequent when instrumentation ended in the cervical rather than thoracic spine; clinical outcomes at final follow-up were also significantly better with EIV-T. They interpret these findings as supporting their hypothesis and crossing the C-T junction to reduce symptomatic caudal ASP after multilevel PCF. Earlier studies had identified leaving C5-6 and C6-7 unfused as a risk factor for ASP after cervical fusion; the authors consider their findings consistent, while noting that their cohort evaluated a posterior-only approach. They describe mechanical effects and progression of underlying disease as proposed contributors to ASP after anterior cervical fusion. Hilibrand et al. reported an annual symptomatic ASP incidence of 2.9% and newly symptomatic ASP in 25.6% within 10 years after anterior cervical fusion. Previously reported risk factors after anterior cervical fusion include reduced plate-tip-to-adjacent-disc distance, preoperative disc degeneration and multilevel fusion. Prasarn et al. found greater adjacent-segment ROM after multilevel than single-level fusion, which might raise ASP risk. In a finite-element study, Hussain et al. found that increased stiffness from multilevel cervical fusion could contribute to both disc and facet-joint degeneration. Lee et al. examined 1358 cervical surgery cases and reported a 3 times greater risk of ASP revision surgery after posterior than anterior cervical fusion. The authors note efforts to identify ASP risks and preventive techniques; in posterior lumbar fusion for degenerative lumbar scoliosis, crossing the thoraco-lumbar junction has been introduced as a possible way to gain rib-cage stabilization. The study has several limitations. Apart from lordosis change, outcomes were not correlated with radiographic findings. A separate study at the authors’ institution associated sagittal malalignment after anterior cervical fusion with more symptomatic ASP; they suggest a subsequent radiographic study to assess whether this applies to posterior fusion. The current study was retrospective, involved one surgeon and included varied surgical indications. They propose a prospective randomized study in a more focused cohort, which could also compare when symptomatic caudal ASP develops in the 2 groups. Their ASP definition excluded patients with milder symptoms managed only with medication or physical therapy; the senior surgeon generally tries noninvasive care before injections. Patients with radiographic ASP but no symptoms were also excluded. Symptomatic cranial ASP was not analyzed: cranial fusion extension could be performed without cranial symptoms during caudal revision to balance fused levels around the lordosis apex, so such extension would not necessarily indicate symptomatic cranial ASP, although a cranial injection might. The groups differed significantly in the number of fused levels. Nevertheless, symptomatic caudal ASP was less frequent in EIV-T despite its longer lever arm, which the authors interpret as a protective effect of crossing the C-T junction. They now seriously consider crossing the cervico-thoracic junction rather than ending at C7 during long instrumented posterior arthrodesis, but caution that ASP avoidance should not dominate level selection. Treating only symptomatic levels may be advisable for young patients seeking to preserve motion when later surgery would not carry undue risk. A shorter construct may likewise be advisable for some frail or very elderly patients if longer fusion poses greater risk. ASP is therefore one of several considerations in choosing levels and counseling patients about future consequences. The authors state that, to their knowledge, theirs is the first comparison of symptomatic caudal ASP after long PCF with versus without crossing this junction. They conclude from this consecutive single-surgeon series, reviewed by 2 independent surgeons, that crossing the C-T junction significantly reduces symptomatic caudal ASP and improves 2-year clinical outcomes, without significant differences in complication rates or operative times. Whether the final instrumented vertebra should be cervical or thoracic remains an individual clinical decision.
